data.title: H. Chorvátová: The meaning of pendants and amulets in early medieval cemeteries
data.excerpt: The archaeologist Hana Chorvátová asks why amulet pendants — shells, rattles, capsules and lunulae — cluster in the graves of children and women. Her answer runs from the early medieval penitentials to grave 226 at Čakajovce, which she reads as the burial of a wise woman. The study was first published in the journal Hieron III in 1998 and appears here with the author's permission.

children.text: We bring our readers an article by the historian and archaeologist Hana Chorvátová which deals with the meaning of pendants in the Early Middle Ages. The article was originally published in the journal Hieron III in 1998 (pp. 106-112) and we publish it on our site with the author's permission.

In seeking to understand prehistoric and early medieval society, archaeology belongs, together with history, among the social sciences. Research into society has brought the insight that society is always co-created by human consciousness. It is not merely the sum of individuals, but also of the links between them. Social interconnectedness may be partly unconscious, and partly may take place precisely at the conscious level of “subjectively intended meanings of behaviour”, in the sphere of ideas and attitudes. From this characterisation of society there follow for the historian the following difficulties. The first lies in the fact that society is not fully manifest, in the sense that in the great majority of social behaviour people do not express to one another the subjectively intended and experienced meanings and values that they attach to their behaviour. This holds for present-day society. Even more veiled remains “past” society. Historians, who are dependent on written sources, simply have to accept that the great majority of the subjectively intended meanings (reasons, motives) of individual social behaviour remained unrecorded. A concept, an idea, an attitude, a feeling and so on — all this is, and this is a further difficulty, the content of the mind. The content of the mind, however, cannot be “known” in the true sense of the word (in the way in which some of the natural sciences, for example, “know”); we can only attempt to “understand” it. Connected with this is also the fact that culture and society cannot be grasped as some fixed object. The complex interweaving of the “outward” expression and the “inward” content of the mind means that in the social sciences it is not possible to “know” connections and causal links as, for instance, in the laws of nature; instead we can achieve a more or less adequate understanding of the links between two or more phenomena (Horský - Seligová 1996, 9, 10, 11). For historians of the Middle Ages it follows from this that in examining the inner content of medieval popular culture — the “image of the world” of medieval man, his way of perceiving the world, the character of his thinking, his collective psychological orientation — the subject of enquiry will not be clearly formulated ideas, but unmanifest patterns of consciousness and action (Gurevič 1996, 13,14).

A wealth of insights from new archaeological excavations with good documentation has opened up new interpretative possibilities for pendants – amulets. The analyses made so far of the occurrence of amulet pendants (shells, rattles, capsules, lunulae and others) show that they are bound in strikingly large numbers to the graves of children and women. This phenomenon can be followed in Frankish cemeteries (Vida 1995, 265; Vallet 1997, 715; Krumphanzlová 1992, 160) and in Great Moravian ones (Stloukal 1964, 110), as well as in cemeteries of a later period (Rejholcová 1976, 215; Klápště 1994, 172). In connection with children's graves it is also important to note that “exceptional finds” — unusual forms of pendants, glass vessels, bottles and the like — occur only in them (Stloukal 1964, 109; Vallet 1997, 715). These are the facts that archaeology places directly before us. In explaining this phenomenon we shall be helped not only by early medieval written sources, but also by the insights of cultural historians and sociologists into the position of children and women in early medieval and medieval society.
I. Amulets in the written sources.

Important information about amulets is to be found in various early medieval ecclesiastical written records, above all in the medieval penitentials. Mentions of amulets are among the most numerous in them and do not disappear even from later sources. Extensive knowledge of amulets from various penitentials was collected long ago by Čeněk Zíbrt in his work Seznam pověr a zvyklostí pohanských z VIII. věku (A List of Pagan Superstitions and Customs of the 8th Century) (Prague 1995, 2nd edition), from which we draw the following data.

children.text: In the ecclesiastical sources amulets are referred to as phylacteria and also as ligaturae. From these sources we learn data that are important for archaeologists, for example that amulets used to be made of various materials: of wood, stone, plants, bone, metal, or else they were merely various ribbons (ligaturae). The penitentials also inform us about the way they were worn. People wore amulets hung round the neck, sewed them into their clothes or wound them round various parts of the body. They also used to hang them on trees and on crosses at crossroads, and tied them round the necks of animals as well. The priests also recorded for us in the penitentials the reasons for wearing amulets. We learn that they had above all a protective function: against illnesses (fever, for instance), for the better healing of wounds, against misfortune and disaster, and also against spells (Zíbrt 1995, 45 - 47).
II. The child in medieval society.

Our knowledge of the attitude of adults towards children in medieval society has deepened considerably since the appearance of Philippe Ariès's pioneering work (1962) (Nodl 1996, 7-29, with further literature there). From some sources, for example written ones (Slivka 1998, 71) or iconographic ones, we might gain the impression that medieval society was indifferent to the fate of children and made no enormous effort to ensure their survival. It even rid itself by force of unwanted children, to which many records in ecclesiastical sources testify (Smetánka 1993, 79). From ethnological observation of indigenous peoples, however, we know that every community, so long as it is not threatened by adverse events (war, crop failure, famine), strives for its generational – lineal – continuation. This is attested to us by many recorded rituals (from the European area as well) connected with childbirth and the birth of a child, whose purpose was to ease the birth and to protect the newborn child and the mother against the evil eye, against infection, illnesses, demons of various kinds and so on (Van Gennep 1996, 47, 50, 54). At first the Church tolerated a number of rituals performed at the baptism of a child in church. So that the infant should not be ill, it was laid on the altar, on a tomb or on a grave — in this way it was to be protected all its life against diseases of the teeth and the eyes. (Gurevič 1994, 20). The rite of laying a child on the altar in case of illness is mentioned also in two legends of St Adalbert (the legends of Canaparius and of Bruno) in connection with Adalbert's sudden illness in early childhood (Nový – Sláma 1987, 123, 153). These rites are condemned only in the penitential of Burchard of Worms (Gurevič 1994, 20).

children.text: It seems that archaeology, too, can contribute in part to shedding light on this problem – the position of children in society. The archaeological excavation of cemeteries in fact provides primary data leading not only to a knowledge of the life of ancient human communities, but also primary information about their notions of life in the “other” world. The most widespread of these notions about the “other” – the second – world is that it resembles ours, but tends to be more pleasant, and that society there is ordered as it is here on earth. Everyone is there, as in his earthly life, once again assigned to the clan, the age class, the occupation and so on that he had on earth. It is then logical that children who had not yet been fully received into the society of the living (in the Middle Ages, for example, unbaptised children) cannot be assigned to any category of the society of the dead (Van Gennep 1996, 142). In the children's graves identified in the cemeteries, children whom society had accepted were buried. Securing a place in the cemetery was in a certain sense a continuation of existence in the settlement – that is, in the community. A place in the cemetery therefore did not belong to undesirable individuals, whether they were adults or children (Smetánka 1993, 79).

The high number of children's graves with the occurrence of various amulets and “exceptional finds” in the cemeteries may suggest to us the emotional attitude of early medieval society towards children, and at the same time the efforts of adults to protect them during life and after death. We should not, however, forget the fact that many children in the graves at present known without finds may have been furnished with various amulets of organic material which, unfortunately, have not survived.
III. The woman in medieval society.

In the following lines we should like to attempt to explain the occurrence of various amulets in the graves of women as well. Among many indigenous peoples and also in archaic societies, women in certain periods of their lives were looked upon as unclean beings (Horváthová 1994, 61). This view of women was adopted by Christianity too. Ecclesiastical formulas of the 11th century refer directly to the Mosaic law on the uncleanness of a woman who has given birth or of a menstruating woman (Gurevič 1994, 20). The unique capacity of women – to give new life – became the basis for the emergence of women's communities, which are documented among many indigenous peoples (Frazer 1994, 512-524) and have also been identified in the Central European area (Wolfram 1933, 141-143). The chief task of these communities was to acquaint and initiate girls and young women in the matters of marriage, childbirth, funeral rites, the efficacy of medicinal plants and so on (Eliade 1997, 188, note 14). Indirect evidence of these communities in Europe is also the fact that in the Middle Ages it was, for instance, out of the question for a man to take part in a birth. Even physicians were forbidden to be present at a birth. Sad is the story of one physician from Hamburg who assisted at a birth disguised as a midwife. In 1521 he was sentenced for this to death by burning (Nodl 1996, 15-16). In the Slavic milieu, too, similar women's communities are indirectly attested (Niederle 1916, 223). Wise women – seeresses – are also mentioned, with whom the whole of human life was bound up. A happy birth, health, good fortune or misfortune and a long life depended on them (Niederle 1916, 217). We may suppose that these pendants are probably a mark of wise women.

children.text: So far we have spoken in general terms of various pendants – amulets as symbols for wise women. At the end of the article it would be fitting to give one example as well: the find of grave 226 from the cemetery at Čakajovce (Rejholcová 1995), which we might perhaps interpret as the grave of a wise woman. Before the interpretation itself, a few remarks. The interpretation of various finds in graves is always very difficult, especially of jewellery; people's relationship to religion, and hence also to the symbolism of jewellery, is an eminently private sphere which we have no possibility of coming to know in detail. It is not possible, however, to work without a certain preliminary hypothesis which guides the gathering of material and the approach to its interpretation (Gurevič 1996, 13). In working out an explanation many pitfalls lie hidden, and the interpretation always remains at the level of hypothesis. As yet no procedures have been worked out for how to verify the symbolic interpretation of archaeological artefacts; how to choose the correct, or at least the more probable, one from among several possibilities; how to proceed in the face of the well-known polysemy of symbols in different communities. So far we have no criteria worked out on which we might rely in interpretation.

In explaining our reflections we have taken our inspiration from the procedure used by C. Renfrew in working out criteria for a sacred feature. He first set out what is known of the activities and acts that form part of ritual ceremonies in sacred architecture. He then pointed out how religious activities may be reflected in archaeological traces and remains. On the basis of these facts he worked out the following criteria which a feature must satisfy if it is to be recognised as sacred: a) the feature attracts attention (crags, stones, trees), b) the feature is bounded (ditches, walls), or has an unusual ground plan, c) elements for focusing attention occur in the feature (an altar), d) objects and traces connected with the performance of ritual are concentrated at the feature (knives, a chalice, the blood of animals and the like). The criteria were worked out for the prehistoric period, but they are valid for the Middle Ages as well – for a church, for example (Renfrew – Bahn 1991, 359-360).

We shall attempt to interpret the status of the woman from grave 226 within the community that buried its dead in the cemetery. It is not possible, however, to work without a certain preliminary hypothesis which guides the gathering of material and the approach to its interpretation (Gurevič 1996, 13). First we should set out the insights offered about society not only by social and cultural anthropology, but also those of historians, archaeologists and scholars of religion.

An important feature of early medieval society is that for the most part it was a society without writing (Gurevič 1996, 23), which allows us to apply some knowledge from research into primitive (archaic) societies. In almost every archaic community there exists the office of priest, sorcerer or shaman, or else this role is sometimes taken over by other persons (smiths or herbalists, for example). The position of these people in society is peculiar. On the one hand they receive honour from the members of the community; on the other, people hold them in awe, even in fear of their exceptional abilities (Murphy 1998, 182 – 185; Soukup 1993, 117). The outward mark of priests, sorcerers or shamans is their dress – their costume. Part of the costume is sometimes various pendants with the function of a talisman. In the Old Testament, in the Book of Exodus, a description of a priest's robe is mentioned. The robe had to be made of violet purple; on its hem there had to be pomegranates of violet and red purple and of crimson, and between them golden bells all around. The dress of shamans was dealt with in detail by M. Eliade (1997, 138-143). Dress as such had an exceptional significance in the Early Middle Ages as well. It signalled a person's social status (Le Goff 1998, 161). Unfortunately, dress – costume – is made of organic materials (textile, wool, leather) and does not survive in our geographical conditions, which is an immense loss and limits our interpretative possibilities. Only the metal parts of the costume can survive.

Noteworthy for our interpretation is a passage in the Saga of the People of Laxárdalur, one of the most important Icelandic sagas, written some time between 1230 and 1260, which, however, tells of events of the 9th, 10th and 11th centuries. The story describes the discovery of a sorceress's grave: “…and she had the floor dug up. Strange black bones were found, a pendant for the neck and a large sorcerer's staff. From this they understood that a sorceress was buried there. They carried her bones away and buried them in a deserted place.” (Lecouteux 1997, 69).

In grave 226 a woman aged 40–60 was buried. Besides the necklace with a pendant, a silver earring, two iron knives, a spindle whorl and a vessel were also placed in her grave (all these objects were laid on the left-hand side of the dead woman). In its dimensions (length 235 cm, width 88 cm, depth 175 cm) the grave pit belonged rather to the more spacious graves in the cemetery (Rejholcová 1995, 8). The grave also belongs to a small group of graves in which the dead were oriented with the head towards the SE – NW, as against the traditional direction NW – SE (Rejholcová 1995, 15,16). It would also be appropriate to draw attention to the fact that in the cemetery in question almost all the graves distinguished by large dimensions are characterised by the reverse orientation (SE – NW). On the basis of horizontal stratigraphy we may state that at the time of burial (the first half of the 9th century) the grave lay at the edge of the cemetery. The pendant that comes from grave 226 is very rare. From the territory of southern Moravia and south-western Slovakia only five examples are so far known. Archaeologists use for it the term “heart-shaped” (Dostál 1966, 54) or also “crescent-shaped” (Štefanovičová 1989, colour plate) and connect them with lunula pendants (Hrubý 1955, 263; Dostál 1966, 54). Lunula pendants are ascribed a connection with the Moon (Královánszky 1959; Váňa 1988, 348), and it is known from various mythologies that the Moon confers exceptional abilities and secures knowledge (Eliade 1958, 163-169). Heart-shaped pendants are generally credited with a cult character (Hanuliak 1997, 476).

On the basis of the insights set out above from the field of cultural and social anthropology and of the circumstances of the find, we may advance the hypothesis that in grave 226 there was evidently buried a woman who held a special position in the community – the oversized grave pit (Eisner 1952, 336), the orientation – but who at the same time also aroused apprehension: the placing at the edge of the cemetery. She may have been precisely a woman with healing abilities and knowledge.
